State Roles and Functions in Regional Large Load
Forecasting
Fritz Kahrl* and Natalie Mims Frick, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
* 3rdRail, Inc.


 States are playing an increasingly important role in reviewing the large load forecasts that transmission utilities
 provide to regional transmission organizations (RTOs), which RTOs use in regional resource adequacy and
 transmission planning. This technical brief provides an overview of emerging state roles and functions in
 regional large load forecasting, focusing on PJM and briefly examining other regions as well.
 PJM implemented significant changes to its long-term load forecasting in early 2026, including opportunities
 for state regulatory review of large load adjustments. This brief examines state review in the context of PJM’s
 large load forecast adjustment process and explores the types of feedback that state agencies and other
 regulatory authorities might provide in their reviews.
 The brief is organized into four sections:
        •     Background – provides an overview of PJM’s long-term load forecasting process, interactions
              between load interconnection and load forecasting, and how long-term load forecasts are used.
        •     PJM’s large load forecast adjustments – describes PJM’s large load forecast adjustment process and
              the role of relevant electric retail regulatory authorities (RERRAs) in reviewing large load forecast
              submissions by electric distribution companies (EDCs) and load serving entities (LSEs).
        •     Large load forecasting and RERRA participation in other ISO/RTO regions – describes RERRA roles in
              load forecasting in other independent system operators (ISOs) and RTOs.
        •     Considerations for RERRA participation in PJM’s load forecast adjustment process – outlines
              considerations for RERRA participation in PJM’s load forecast adjustments, how RERRAs might
              coordinate their participation, and potential clarifications, questions, and areas of feedback for PJM.



      1. Background
This section provides background on PJM’s long-term load forecast; its use in resource adequacy, transmission
planning, interconnection; and its use in and implications for other recent PJM initiatives related to large loads
and transmission planning.

1.1 PJM’s Long-Term Load Forecast
Each year, PJM develops a 20-year forecast of hourly demand for each PJM zone. 1 This load forecast is based on
a multi-variable regression model that incorporates weather conditions, economic drivers, trends in end-use


1 Historically, PJM’s load forecast appears to have been limited to coincident and non-coincident peak and annual energy demand. More

recently, PJM appears to have moved to hourly load forecasts, consistent with a 2022 review of and recommendations to improve its
load forecast model by Itron (2022 PJM Model Review). For more detail on PJM’s load forecasting methods, see its PJM Manual 19: Load
Forecasting and Analysis. The information in this section is based on revision 38 (effective date December 17, 2025) of Manual 19.
                                                                                                                                        1
 efficiency, distributed solar generation, and electric vehicles. PJM adjusts the load forecasts generated by its
model to account for large load additions and peak shaving programs.

PJM uses historical weather data to simulate distributions of monthly non-coincident and coincident peak load
forecasts for each zone. From this distribution, PJM selects median (50/50) and 10th percentile (90/10) values
for each season to use in its resource adequacy mechanism and transmission planning and expansion.

Changes to PJM’s model and load forecast adjustments are reviewed by the Load Analysis Subcommittee and
Planning Committee. Members of the Planning Committee may request a review of the load forecast.

1.2 Uses of PJM’s Long-Term Load Forecast
PJM’s uses its long-term load forecasts primarily as inputs to its resource adequacy mechanism and in
transmission planning studies (Figure 1).
    • Resource adequacy – as inputs to the loss-of-load expectation (LOLE) analysis in PJM’s LOLE Study and
       to clear PJM’s capacity auction – the Reliability Pricing Mechanism (RPM).
    • Transmission planning and expansion – as inputs to transmission models used in PJM’s Regional
       Transmission Expansion Plan (RTEP) and generator interconnection.

Figure 1. Key Uses of PJM’s Long-Term Load Forecast in Resource Adequacy and Transmission Planning and Expansion,
and Interactions Between Load Interconnection, Load Forecasting, and RTEP




Load interconnection, which is managed by transmission and distribution utilities, provides data inputs for large
load adjustments, directly interacts with the RTEP process, and has a more indirect relationship with resource
adequacy (see box, below).



                                                                                                                    2
  Load Interconnection, Resource Adequacy, and Transmission Planning
 A large load wishing to obtain electric service must first contact the transmission or distribution utility
 to request service. In PJM, the utility is responsible for conducting studies to determine what new
 infrastructure is needed to connect the load. Utilities typically do not evaluate the resource adequacy
 impacts of large loads in load interconnection, though in non-restructured states they may use
 interconnection requests and milestones in the load forecasts used in resource planning and
 procurement.

 If the utility identifies reliability issues that require new transmission infrastructure, the utility submits
 these transmission projects (“supplemental projects”) for review by Subregional RTEP Committees
 and, in some cases, the Transmission Expansion Advisory Committee (TEAC) under PJM’s Attachment
 M-3 process. The M-3 process is separate from RTEP but feeds into it, as supplemental projects are
 included in the base transmission case in the next RTEP planning cycle. Utilities often do not provide
 detailed descriptions of how loads are modeled in load interconnection, making it difficult to
 determine the balance between large load-driven transmission issues that are addressed in RTEP
 versus being first addressed in load interconnection.*

 * In general, it appears that most incremental, near-term reliability issues within a transmission utility’s service
 territory that are caused by the addition of a new large load will be addressed through interconnection and
 supplemental projects, though larger, longer-term issues may be addressed through RTEP. For examples of
 utility interconnection guidelines, see those for AEP and Dominion.

In capacity markets and transmission planning, PJM uses load forecasts to identify resource and transmission
needs. PJM allocates costs for the capacity auction and for transmission based on metered historical rather than
forecasted demand. 2 Still, load forecasts have a significant influence on the timing, location, and magnitude of
generation and transmission investments and thus on the costs that consumers eventually pay. The cost impact
of inaccurate large load forecasts may be borne regionally rather than locally. 3

1.3 PJM’s Long-Term Load Forecast in Recent Initiatives4
Large load forecasts have implications for several other recent PJM initiatives, including:
    • Reliability Resource Initiative (RRI) and Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT)
    • Reliability backstop procurement (RBP)
    • Bring-your-own new generation (BYONG)
    • Non-firm transmission service

2 Cost allocation for PJM’s capacity market is covered in PJM Manual 19: Load Forecasting and Analysis; cost allocation for transmission is

covered in PJM Manual 14B: PJM Region Transmission Planning Process.
3 The extent to which cost shifting occurs as a result of load forecast error can often be subtle and related to the timing of changes in load

ratio shares, which are determined by historical metered load rather than forecasted load. However, as a simple example consider two
utilities (Utilities A and B) that allocate transmission costs based on load ratio share. Each utility accounted for 50% of metered load in the
previous year and the annual transmission revenue requirement (ATRR) was $200 million, with each utility paying $100 million. Utility A
forecasts a new 100 MW data center load that triggers new transmission needs and a $10 million increase in the ATRR. Utility B does not
forecast any load growth. Permitting is more arduous than anticipated and the data center customer eventually cancels the project.
Utility A and B still account for 50% of metered demand but the ATRR has increased to $210 million, increasing Utility B’s share of the
ATRR to $105 million.
4 The terms and descriptions in this section are as of mid-June 2026. PJM has changed some of the terms and proposed approaches since.

                                                                                                                                             3
     •    Connect and manage
    •    Long-term regional transmission planning (LTRTP)

In most instances, the key question for large load forecasts in these initiatives is which large loads to include in
the forecasts used for generation procurement, capacity market clearing, and transmission planning.

Reliability resource initiative (RRI) and expedited interconnection track (EIT). RRI and EIT both aim to fast track
generator interconnection to resolve projected near-term gaps in resource adequacy. RRI was a one-time
initiative, approved by FERC in 2025, that allowed up to 50 projects to be fast tracked and join an already-in-
progress interconnection study cluster. 5 EIT is a two-year initiative, approved by FERC in 2026, that will fast track
generator projects that demonstrate an ability to achieve commercial operation within three years. 6 The need
for both of these initiatives was informed by PJM’s long-term load forecasts.

Reliability backstop procurement. RBP is a one-time, transitional process to procure generation capacity for
large loads. The purpose is to close the gap between supply and demand in PJM’s 2029 capacity auction. 7 RBP
will have two phases. In the first phase, PJM will act as a facilitator for bilateral contracting between buyers and
suppliers. In the second phase, PJM will procure any remaining capacity needed to meet a procurement target.
The procurement target will be based on the 2026 forecast year’s 2029 summer large load forecast for each
zone minus the 2026 summer large load forecast. Although not explicitly stated, the large load forecast used to
set the procurement target should be based on PJM’s modifications to large load adjustments submitted by
EDCs/LSEs (“firm” additions to the base load forecast, see Section 2.3). PJM clarifies that the load forecast used
in RBP will exclude generation and load from entities that have fixed resource requirements (FRRs).8

Bring-your-own new generation. BYONG, approved by the PJM Board in the large load CIFP, creates a voluntary
expedited interconnection process for large loads that are paired with new generation. PJM does not appear to
have developed a proposal for BYONG yet. 9 In theory, BYONG load should not be included in the RBP’s
procurement target. However, BYONG load and generation should be included in the RPM and in RTEP except
under specific circumstances. 10

Non-firm transmission service. In December 2025, FERC directed PJM to file a proposal for non-firm
transmission service for co-located load and generation. 11 Non-firm transmission service allows a customer to
connect to the transmission system before all network upgrades required to reliably deliver power to the load

5 For more on the RRI and its results, see “PJM Chooses 51 Generation Resource Projects To Address Near-Term Electricity Demand

Growth,” PJM Inside Lines, May 2, 2025.
6 For more on the EIT, see PJM’s Expedited Interconnection Track Procedures.
7 PJM’s Critical Issue Fast Path – Reliability Backstop Procurement provides more detail on its proposed approach.
8 FRRs allow LSEs to opt-out of PJM’s capacity market by demonstrating adequate resources to meet their peak coincident demand plus

PJM’s planning reserve margin. In delivery year 2026/2027, FRRs were equivalent to 11% of total capacity cleared in the RPM (see Tables
4 and 5 of PJM’s 2026/2027 Base Residual Auction Report).
9 SPP’s FERC-approved Load Limited Resource Interconnection Service (LLRIS) may provide a reference for the design of these kinds of

expedited interconnection processes for co-located load and generation, though as described in Section 3 there are important differences
between SPP and PJM.
10 For the RPM, PJM may provide a pathway for large loads to opt-out of the PRM if they have adequacy generation to cover their peak

demand plus the planning reserve margin. For RTEP, load and generation could be excluded from the load forecast if they are co-located
and the large load customer has committed to limit withdrawals from the transmission system to a maximum (MW) amount.
11 See Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 and EL25-49-001 (193 FERC ¶ 61,217) at https://elibrary.ferc.gov/eLibrary/.

                                                                                                                                      4
 are completed, with the customer agreeing to be curtailed when needed. PJM’s proposal for non-firm
transmission service remains in a stakeholder process. 12 Non-firm transmission service could be temporary or
permanent. Co-located load and generation with permanent non-firm transmission service should not be
included in the load forecast used in RPM or RTEP, though customers with temporary non-firm service should be
included.

Connect and manage. Separately, PJM’s Board approved a “connect and manage” mechanism that would allow
loads – regardless of whether they have co-located generation – to come online before they have supporting
generation or transmission if they agree to be curtailable when needed. Connect and manage is thus a broader
form of non-firm generation and transmission service. PJM does not appear to have developed a proposal for
connect and manage yet. 13 Like non-firm transmission service, the non-firm service resulting from connect and
manage could be temporary or permanent, and should be included in the load forecasts used RPM or RTEP if
temporary and should not be included if permanent.

Long-term regional transmission planning. LTRTP is PJM’s Order 1920-compliant transmission planning process,
which PJM submitted to FERC in December 2025. 14 PJM’s proposal did not describe whether and how large load
forecast adjustments would be included in the load forecast or in the scenarios used in the LTRTP’s identification
of new transmission needs. 15


1.4 Potential Impacts of FERC’s Show Cause Order on PJM”s Large Load Adjustment Process
On June 18, 2026, FERC ordered PJM and its member transmission owners to show cause, under section 206 of
the Federal Power Act, why its existing tariff is just and reasonable without addressing several issues related to
large loads, and to explain how they would revise the tariff if FERC were to find it unjust and unreasonable. 16
The first two of these issues may have significant implications for PJM’s large load adjustment process:
     (a) “the application process, study procedures, and ongoing operational requirements that apply to Eligible
         Customers seeking transmission service on behalf of large loads;
     (b) additional transparency concerning the Network Upgrade costs to provide transmission service to
         Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads, a pro forma cost recovery agreement between PJM, the
         relevant transmission owner and Eligible Customer taking transmission service on behalf of the large
         load to mitigate the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers, and a mechanism to ensure
         such payments are appropriately credited towards transmission owners’ transmission revenue
         requirements consistent with the Commission’s cost-of-service regulations.”



12 PJM’s initial proposal received significant pushback from stakeholders. See Ethan Howland, “PJM data center colocation plan takes fire

from Vistra, data center group, others,” Utility Dive, March 27, 2026.
13 Again, SPP’s proposed conditional high impact large load (CHILL) service might provide a reference.
14 See PJM’s compliance filing for more detail on its proposal.
15 Presumably, only firm adjustments would be included in the Core LT Needs scenarios, whereas non-firm adjustments could be included

in the Additional LT Needs scenarios.
16 The two additional issues in the order were: “(c) transmission services that reflect Eligible Customers taking transmission service on

behalf of flexible large loads that are willing and able to limit their use of the transmission system under certain conditions; and (d) the
rates, terms, and conditions of service applicable to interconnection customers serving electrically proximate large load or co-located
load.” See FERC’s June 18, 2026 Order Instituting Proceeding with PJM and its member transmission owners.
                                                                                                                                          5
 There are multiple ways in which PJM and member transmission owners could comply with the show cause
order, ranging from more incremental changes that build upon the existing process to larger, structural changes
in PJM’s load interconnection and load forecast adjustment processes. The show cause order could also lead to
changes in the risks of large load forecast error, for instance by direct assigning a larger share of interconnection
facility and transmisison costs to interconnecting large loads. In thinking through RERRA roles and functions in
PJM’s large load forecast adjustments, it will be helpful to keep in mind this show cause order and how it might
shape the adjustment process going forward.

    2. PJM’s Large Load Forecast Adjustments
PJM’s large load adjustment process incorporates load growth that is not captured in forecast models into its
long-term load forecast. PJM requests adjustments from EDCs/LSEs each year and modifies these adjustments to
account for uncertainty before including in its long-term load forecast.


 Large Load Forecast “Adjustments”
 Language around PJM’s load forecast adjustments can be confusing. PJM uses the term “adjustment” to refer to the
 submissions of large load forecasts* from EDCs/LSEs, because these forecasts are adjustments to PJM’s base load
 forecasts. However, “adjustment” could also refer to PJM’s subsequent modifications to the large load forecasts it
 receives from EDCs/LSEs. For clarity, we use the term “adjustment” to refer to EDC/LSE large load forecasts and
 “modification” to refer to PJM’s changes to those forecasts.*

 * PJM typically refers to large load forecasts as “demand requests.” PJM also appears to use the term “modification” to refer to
 its downward revisions to EDC/LSE demand requests.


Before 2022, forecast adjustments through this process were relatively small – around 1 GW or less (Figure 2,
below). 17 However, since 2022 they have increased significantly, especially in the 2025 and 2026 load forecasts
(Figure 2). PJM’s 2021 load forecast 18 had almost no large load growth from 2022 to 2036. By contrast, for PJM’s
2026 load forecast summer peak demand adjustments were 11 GW for year 2026, 39 GW for 2030, 69 GW for
2035, 83 GW for 2040, and 87 GW for the last year of the load forecast in 2046. For reference, PJM’s summer
peak demand in 2025 was 154 GW. 19




17 The adjustments in the first part of this section draw on Table B-9 in PJM’s Long-Term Load Forecast Report series and appear to

include upward and downward adjustments for large loads and downward adjustments for voltage optimization. The first year in which
PJM had a substantial upward adjustment was in the 2014 load forecast, due to data center growth in the Dominion zone.
18 The year here refers to the first year of the forecast. PJM releases its Long-Term Load Forecast Report in January of the first year

covered under the forecast. For instance, the 2021 report was released in January 2021 and 2021 is the first year covered under the
forecast.
19 This value is from the Weather Normalized Peaks spreadsheet.

                                                                                                                                          6
 Figure 2. Large Load Adjustments to the PJM Long-Term Load Forecast, Forecast Years 2009-2026




Figure notes and source: Each series in Figures 2 and 3 is a 15-year or 20-year load forecast. The first point in the series is
the year of the forecast. For instance, the 2026 forecast begins in 2026 and extends over 20 years, from 2026 to 2046. PJM
appears to have moved from a 15-year to a 20-year forecast in 2025. All data are from PJM’s Long-Term Load Forecast
Report series (historical reports available under “Previous Reports”).

2.1 Large Load Adjustment Process and RERRA Review
Historically, PJM has solicited large load adjustments from EDCs/LSEs on an annual basis. In early to mid-July,
PJM sends requests for adjustments to EDCs/LSEs. Responses are required in September so the results can be
included in the Load Analysis Subcommittee meeting in September/October. After the results are presented,
PJM reviews and modifies load forecast adjustment submissions, making additional requests for information
from EDCs/LSEs as needed. In October/November, PJM announces the final large load adjustments at a Load
Analysis Subcommittee meeting. PJM requires EDCs/LSEs to provide written documentation of their load
forecast adjustments in November/December. In December/January, PJM publishes its load forecast in the
Long-Term Load Forecast Report. Table 1 shows the schedule for large load forecast adjustments in 2025.

The large load CIFP stakeholder process created an additional step in the large load adjustment process for
review of forecast adjustments by RERRAs — public utility commissions (PUCs), municipal boards, and
cooperative (co-op) boards. PJM’s proposed revisions to its Load Forecasting and Analysis manual (Manual 19)
indicate that the core adjustment process will remain unchanged, with three additions. 20 First, EDCs/LSEs must
inform PJM of intent to submit requests by August 1 each year. Second, the RERRA review must occur before
EDCs/LSEs submit their adjustments to PJM in September/October. Third, an independent consultant will
conduct a parallel large load forecast, using a combination of EDC/LSE adjustment requests and its assessment
of national trends.

RERRA review is voluntary, though EDCs/LSEs that submit adjustment requests must provide an opportunity for
review. The EDC/LSE must indicate in its submission if the RERRA waived the opportunity to review. PJM does
not specify a timeline for RERRA review, but the EDC/LSE must specify when the adjustment was shared with the
RERRA and if the EDC/LSE and RERRA held any meetings to discuss the adjustment.

PJM does not provide specific guidance on the kinds of feedback that it expects RERRAs will provide. EDC/LSE
requests must document what feedback the RERRA provided, though the EDC/LSE is not required to incorporate
the feedback. EDC/LSE requests must include verification from the RERRA that EDC/LSE description of its process
and feedback is accurate. PJM will disclose whether a RERRA reviewed adjustment requests but will not disclose
feedback provided by the RERRA. PJM may not consider adjustment requests valid unless EDCs/LSEs document
RERRA review.




20 The information in this section is based on the proposed revisions to Appendix B of this manual that were released on May 1, 2026.

PJM’s proposal may change with stakeholder feedback.
                                                                                                                                        8
 2.2 Requirements for Load Forecast Adjustment Requests
PJM’s proposed revisions to Manual 19 define large loads for the purposes of load adjustment as 50 MW or
larger. 21 PJM does not have a required methodology for EDC/LSE large load adjustments but does set
requirements for adjustment requests. Each EDC/LSE’s approach to forecasting large load adjustments must be
documented, made publicly available through PJM’s website, and justified to PJM staff and stakeholders if
necessary.

EDCs/LSEs submit large load adjustment requests through PJM’s Excel-based adjustment request template. In
this template, EDCs/LSEs are required to provide detailed project-specific information on project status and
characteristics, in addition to expected load. This information includes:

         “… facility owner, location, status of site control and permitting, load type (if data center, type of
         data center if known), project demand characteristics (includes online date, and capacity and
         demand over time), project configuration (network vs co-located) project stage (Electric Service
         Obligation or ESO, Construction Commitment or CC , or Other), and financial responsibility
         (including information on minimum demand provisions, length of term, exit fees, etc.).” 22

The actual load forecast information required in the adjustment request template includes large load annual and
monthly capacity, annual and monthly peak demand, and monthly energy demand. An EDC/LSE might use a
variety of approaches to calculate these values (see Appendix 1 for examples). For example, an EDC/LSE might
include load with an existing electric service agreement (ESA), including specified monthly capacity and energy
demand, in its forecast with limited to no modification. Similarly, an EDC/LSE might include load that has only
made an interconnection request in its adjustment request but modify (discount) it and use assumptions to fill in
uncertain or unknown values.

Analytically, there are four key factors that EDCs/LSEs in the PJM region use to modify or calculate large loads’
requested capacity and energy demand: probability factor, utilization rate, ramp rate, and load factor. The box
below describes these factors and clarifies PJM’s use of the terms “capacity” and “demand” in large load
forecast adjustments.



 Key Concepts in Large Load Forecast Adjustments in PJM

 Capacity. Capacity is the maximum capacity requested by large load customers. For instance, if a load
 requests 100 MW of capacity, it can consume a maximum of 100 MW.

 Demand. Demand is the projected actual summer peak consumption by large loads. For instance,
 large load customers might request 1,000 MW of maximum capacity but only consume a maximum of
 700 MW during summer peak.



21 Adjustments for loads smaller than 50 MW may be included on a case-by-case basis.
22 The current template requires less detailed information.

                                                                                                                    9
 Probability factor. Probability factor is the probability of an interconnection request achieving
commercial operation. For instance, if only half of interconnection requests have historically achieved
commercial operation, the probability factor for interconnection requests might be 50%.

Utilization rate. Utilization rate (also utilization factor) is the ratio between demand and capacity, or
the share of requested capacity that the load actually uses. If customers request 1,000 MW but only
use 700 MW, the average utilization rate is 70% (= 700 MW / 1,000 MW). PJM uses a default
minimum utilization rate of 70% to modify forecasts. Utilization rate and probability factor are
distinct, though are sometimes confused and combined into a single factor.

Ramp rate. Ramp rate is the expected amount of time for large loads to reach their full requested
capacity or demand, in months or years. For instance, in 2026 a customer may request 100 MW of
new service, with an expected commercial operation date of January 2029. If the customer has a
ramp rate of 36 months, the project will reach its full capacity in January 2032. Ramp rates are often
assumed to be linear, which means that each month the project’s capacity would increase by 2.78
MW (= 100 MW ÷ 36 months). PJM uses a default 36 month ramp rate.

Load factor. Load factor is the ratio between average and peak demand. It can be used to estimate
energy demand from peak demand and vice versa. For instance, a customer with an annual load
factor of 80% and an expected (actual) peak demand of 70 MW will have an average demand of 56
MWa (= 70 MW × 0.80) and an annual energy demand of 490,560 MWh/year (= 56 MW × 8,760
hours/year). Load factors can be defined over any time period but will typically be for months,
seasons, or a year. Average demand is calculated by dividing energy demand by the number of hours
in the time horizon. In this case 56 MW = 490,560 MWh/yr ÷ 8,760 hours/year.

Example. A utility receives large load requests for 5,000 MW of capacity. Historically, 50% of these
requests have achieved commercial operation. The loads that achieve commercial operation are
expected to have an average utilization rate of 70%, an average ramp rate of 36 months, and an
average load factor of 80% (monthly and annual). During the first three years, expected peak demand
will increase by 49 MW per month (= 5,000 MW × 0.50 × 0.70 ÷ 36 months) and will reach 1,750 MW
(= 5,000 MW × 0.50 × 0.70) by year 4 (end of month 36), as shown in the figure below. Expected
annual energy demand will increase by 4,088 GWh/year (= 49 MW/month × 12 months × 0.80 × 8760
hours/year × 1 GWh/1,000 MWh) and reach 12,264 GWh/year (= 1,750 MW × 0.80 × 8760 hours/year
× 1 GWh/1,000 MWh) by year 4.

2.3 PJM Review and Modification
PJM uses a two-part process to modify load adjustments. In the first part (“part 1”), PJM determines whether
requested adjustments may have already been captured in its load forecast model and, if so, removes them
from the request. Manual 19 does not specify how PJM makes these determinations. 23

In the second part, PJM reviews remaining adjustment requests and modifies them based on interconnection
status, performance characteristics, and industry trends. Going forward, the second part of PJM’s process will
also rely on a review by a third-party consultant (see Section 2.4). Adjustment requests with in-service dates that
are within three years of the initial forecast year – the time horizon used for the RPM – must have an electric
service obligation (ESO), a construction commitment (CC), or a long-term supply commitment plus a financial
commitment (Other) to be considered “firm” and included in the load forecast (see box). PJM also appears to
consider requests that have an ESO/CC but have in-service dates longer than three years from the forecast year
as firm and eligible to be included in the forecast. 24 PJM may still derate firm requests, as described below.
PJM categorizes adjustment requests with expected three- to eight-year in-service dates that do not have an
ESO/CC as “Other” (see box), and requires supporting documentation on project milestones and probability
factors to include these loads in the forecast as non-firm demand. 25 If EDCs/LSEs do not provide a probability



23 In other documents, PJM notes that it “reviews economic forecast to determine if load shift is captured” and “obtains hourly load

history to isolate impact and avoid double counting” (see Load Forecast Development & Use in PJM). However, as described in
subsequent text, in practice it appears as if PJM assumed that all non-data center industrial adjustments were already included in the
base load forecast. It also appears that PJM removes data center load from its regressions in calculating the base load forecast, to avoid
double counting.
24 The Load Adjustment Request Implementation document states that, “For identified projects coming online in more than three years

CAISO. In California, a state agency – the California Energy Commission (CEC) – generates the base and large
load forecasts used in the state’s resource adequacy program and in CAISO transmission planning. The CEC
collects information on large load projects from utilities and groups them into three categories: (1) projects that
have an electric service agreement; (2) projects that have a formal interconnection request but have not yet
completed interconnection studies; and (3) inquiries.

The CEC uses confidence levels (probability factors) to de-rate projects within each group for low, mid, and high
forecast scenarios: low, mid, and high (Table 3). In 2025, it calculated the large load to be included in load
forecasts by multiplying a project’s requested capacity by the confidence level, a utilization factor (67%), and a
default ramp rate (7 years) if project-specific ramp rates are not available. 30 The mid scenarios are used in
planning for system-wide resource adequacy and transmission needs, whereas the high scenarios are used in
planning for local needs. 31

    4. Considerations for RERRA Participation in PJM’s Load Forecast Adjustment
       Process
RERRA participation in PJM’s proposed load forecast adjustment process involves review of EDC/LSE adjustment
requests, but may also involve regional coordination among RERRAs and requesting clarifications, asking
questions, and providing feedback to PJM on its modification methods. This section is organized into these three
areas: (1) RERRA review of EDC/LSE adjustment requests, (2) regional coordination, and (3) potential
clarifications, questions, and feedback to PJM. A central theme explored in the RERRA review section (section
4.1) is how to identify an appropriate level of effort in RERRA reviews, to ensure the RERRA is meeting its
oversight responsibilities but avoiding duplication of PJM’s efforts. Some amount of EDC/LSE reporting and
RERRA verification may help increase transparency and accountability.

4.1 RERRA Review of EDC/LSE Adjustment Requests
PJM has not specified the type of load forecast adjustment review or feedback it is seeking from RERRAs. RERRA
review could range from none or relatively minimal to extensive and staff-intensive. RERRAs can consider three
questions to help determine the desired level of effort along this spectrum.

Question 1. What information is PJM already collecting and verifying from EDCs/LSEs and what information does
PJM ultimately need?

PJM plans to collect most of the information it needs to verify and modify large load adjustment requests from
EDCs/LSEs in its large load request template and additional requests for information, though PJM recognizes
that RERRA rules may limit what information EDCs/LSEs can share with PJM. 42 PJM’s proposed approach does
not appear to request that EDCs/LSEs share individual contracts. It is not clear how much effort PJM will expend
to verify contracts and any parameters (utilization rates, ramp rates) provided by EDCs/LSEs.

Ultimately, PJM needs three kinds of information from EDCs/LSEs: (1) information to assess duplicative requests
and duplication within its baseline forecast (e.g., facility name, type, size, and whether it has similar request
elsewhere in PJM); 43 (2) information to assess the certainty of adjustment requests and determine firm/non-
firm status and, for non-firm, probability factors (e.g., project milestones); (3) information to derate requested
capacity and convert capacity to energy (e.g., utilization rates, ramp rates, load factors).

Question 2. What will RERRA review entail and what will the final feedback product look like (bearing in mind
staff and other resource constraints)?

Question 3. How will or could RERRA feedback link with other processes, such as resource planning, utility large
load reporting requirements, and large load registries?

Several of the activities in Table 5 overlap with existing processes, including:

    •    Resource planning. Load forecasting is an integral part of resource planning and distribution system
         planning. In aggregate, the information that PJM is requesting from EDCs/LSEs would likely also be
         developed and made public through a resource planning proceeding. RERRAs could consider how to
         incorporate reviews of large load interconnections in proceedings related to resource and distribution
         system planning.
    •    State reporting requirements. Several states have requirements for regular EDC/LSE reporting on large
         loads, including Arkansas, North Carolina, and Georgia. 44 Other states have legislation authorizing and
         requiring PUC oversight and reporting on large load forecasts. These include Pennsylvania’s HB1924 and
         New Jersey’s Bill S4938/S3370. These reporting requirements may overlap with the large load
         adjustment process and the information that PJM is requesting from EDCs/LSEs.
    •    Large load registries and databases. Some states have laws, regulations, or initiatives to develop large
         load registries or databases, which may contain most if not all of the information EDCs/LSEs use to
         develop their adjustment requests. For instance, Maryland’s HB1532 will require the Maryland Publish
         Service Commission to develop a large load customer registry by July 1, 2027.

Aligning RERRA review with these activities may help to avoid duplicative effort, though it may be challenging to
do so in the 2026 cycle due to time constraints. RERRAs could consider providing feedback to PJM on the timing
of LLA and the expectations for RERRA review to better align PJM’s forecasting with relevant state proceedings.

4.2 Regional Coordination
Given that the impacts of large load forecast error are of regional concern, there may be areas of common
interest among states that would support regional coordination on large load adjustments, including:

    •    Coordination on review methods. Discuss RERRA approaches to review (less effort) or agreement on
         consistency for some or all of RERRA review approaches (more effort).

reuquirements on large loads for Duke (North Carolina), and quarterly reporting requirements for Georgia Power.

     •   Common understanding. Develop a common understanding of PJM’s approach and methods, EDC/LSE
        terminology and practices around large load interconnection, and EDC/LSE methods for large load
        forecasting and adjustment requests.
    •   Agreement on minimum thresholds. Agree on a minimum level of financial commitment (e.g.,

An expanded group of the Organization of PJM States, Inc. (OPSI) Load Forecast Working Group might provide a

4.3 Potential Clarifications, Questions, and Feedback for PJM
Based on this memo, nearer-term clarification, questions, and feedback for PJM might include:

    •   Financial commitment and firmness. Does PJM have a minimum level of financial commitment from
        customers that would be required to be included in the firm forecast, or is any commitment acceptable?
        Does the customer need to have provided initial collateral or payment?
    •   Modification parameters. Is PJM planning to make its default probability factors, utilization rates, ramp
        rates, and load factors more empirical over time? If so, how? Is there a minimum amount of data that
        PJM will require that EDCs/LSEs have to use their own parameters? Would it be worthwhile to add a
        delay parameter that accounts for average delays in connecting projects, similar to ERCOT’s (18-month)
        parameter?
    •   Use of adjustment requests. How is PJM planning to use the non-firm forecasts in transmission planning
        and is PJM planning to report on how it has used RERRA review?

Clarifications, questions, and feedback will change as PJM’s load adjustment process continues to evolve.

 Appendix 1: Milestones, Agreements, and Commitments
PJM’s approach to modifying large load forecast adjustments relies on an assessment of completed milestones,
agreements, and financial commitments in the load interconnection process. In PJM, this process is managed by
transmission and distribution utilities.

Generally, the load interconnection process begins with a non-committal inquiry (Figure A-1). In the second
step, the customer submits a formal interconnection request and the utility studies the request to determine
the infrastructure needed to reliably connect the customer’s load. Some utilities require the customer to sign an
agreement, and most utilities require a study deposit, before commencing interconnection studies. Some
utilities require increasing levels of financial commitment throughout the load interconnection study process.

Figure A-1. General Description of Steps, Milestones, Agreements, and Commitments in Load Interconnection




Once interconnection studies are complete, the customer must decide whether to continue with the project. If
the customer decides to continue, some utilities require the customer to commit to fund interconnection
facilities and any needed transmission or distribution infrastructure. Some utilities also require customers to sign
an electric service agreement (ESA) at this stage, specifying longer-term commitments. In PJM, once the
customer has committed to the project there is also an additional step in which utilities must submit any
transmission projects related to the customer’s request in the M-3 process (“integration into transmission
planning” in figure A-1).




                                                                                                                 23
 The two points at which customers generally sign agreements and make payments are before interconnection
studies begin and before work begins on any new infrastructure needed for the customer. PJM’s ESO/CC
requirement targets the latter stage, in which the customer has made financially binding commitments to fund
the grid infrastructure needed for its project.

As described in Appendix 2, EDCs/LSEs in PJM have different terminology for the agreements and financial
commitments at each stage of the load interconnection process, making it somewhat difficult to compare them.
